    1996 – now

    A life, in the order it happened

    Thirty years, nineteen homes, twenty-three countries and one winter spent walking across a continent. Scroll.

    1996

    A street in Otley

    He was born in January, in Leeds, and home was a market town in Wharfedale — the first house lasted less than a year. Then another, a few streets over — the years that come back not as events but as weather.

    2003 – 2013

    Otley, and a bedroom with a screen in it

    West Busk Lane. Two dogs, Oscar and Kelly. Four guinea pigs — Pippin, Lily, Goldie and Violet — and Rosie the cat, who had moved house with them.

    And then, from about eleven, the screen. Call of Duty first, played properly and competitively, then League of Legends — where he got very good indeed. Challenger, the top rank, in both three-a-side and five-a-side.

    In June 2013, at seventeen, he was the jungler for a team called Team Mistral, under the handle G Man. The roster is still on Leaguepedia. The mid-laner was a German teenager who went on to play professionally.

    He was also smoking a great deal of weed, and taking mephedrone. That is the same stretch of years, the same bedrooms and the same friends — one of whom he met through it. It belongs in the story rather than beside it.

    Challenger3v3 and 5v5
    June 2013Team Mistral
    17years old

    September 2013

    Seventeen

    His mother died. She was fifty-one.

    The family moved along the same street afterwards — roughly the same view from a different window, which is its own particular kind of grief.

    Everything in this record divides quietly into before that and after it.

    2014 – 2018

    Leeds, and the people start arriving

    Hyde Park first, then Woodhouse, a year in Halifax on a credit-risk team, then back for a final year.

    This is where the friends begin — the housemates and the coursemates — and most of them are still here at the end of the story.

    2018 – 2019

    London, and then no address at all

    A house in Poplar he can no longer place — not the street, not the number. Then Mile End, where he wrote that the housemates felt like a real family, and ten days later that it was his last weekend there.

    Then nine weeks in eight or nine hostels, living out of a bag in a city he already lived in. The first rehearsal for everything after.

    24 September – 28 November 2019

    He walked out of the airport

    Not from a station or a hotel. From the perimeter of Charles de Gaulle, heading east with everything he owned on his back.

    France, Germany, Austria, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Bulgaria. Thirty to fifty kilometres on an ordinary day, three days near seventy, over the Tauern in late October on foot and alone.

    Every single day he named after a record.

    28 November 2019

    Sofia

    Forty-seven and a half kilometres into the city, and that was the end of it.

    He titled the last day 'Allelujah! Don't Bend! Ascend!

    “I got the coach from Sofia to Istanbul, I was done.”

    December 2019 – January 2020

    Istanbul, and then India

    Being done with walking turned out not to mean being done. A fortnight in Istanbul and a hundred and fifty-seven kilometres run through it, first out of Sultanahmet and then from the Asian side.

    Then a flight out before Christmas. Rishikesh and the Ganges, Goa and the sand, Jaipur, Mumbai. Home to Otley by the sixteenth of January, where he logged a run called Welcome Home.

    March – November 2020

    A valley, and then a hill above Athens

    He went to his father's house in Wensleydale as the country closed, and stayed most of the year. Tree-planting, dry-stone walling, trench-digging. He called it his Walden.

    Days before it all shut, he had run his longest race — 52.6 km in seven hours and fourteen minutes. It appears in no written record anywhere; only Strava kept it.

    It was a lonely year and he says so at the time. What lifted it was not the running. It was a handful of long conversations in January, and a friend pointing the irony out to his face: he had crossed a continent alone to cure loneliness, and what cured it was talking to someone.

    Then in October he went to Athens by himself, sat on Filopappou Hill looking across at the Acropolis, and finally had the reckoning with his mother's death that had been waiting seven years.

    He took the job that week. In November he wrote: I am finally me.

    2020 – 2022

    Back to Leeds

    A house on Shaw Lane with real turnover, people arriving and leaving over eighteen months.

    One housemate came for the last three months. Nearly four years later they would be living together again, which nobody could have known at the time.

    December 2022 – January 2026

    The house family

    Three years and a month at Thornbury Avenue — the longest he has stayed anywhere as an adult, and the household his journals simply call the house family.

    The tenancy ended on the thirty-first of January 2026, and that was the end of Leeds.

    Late January – March 2026

    Seven cities, as a test

    It was not a holiday. He had already decided on Lisbon and went to America to make sure — in his own words, to make sure I'm not making a bad decision.

    Beach yoga at dawn in Miami, the run club there twice, salsa in the San Fernando Valley, line dancing by the marina in San Francisco. He flew home overnight on the twenty-second of March.

    From May 2026

    Chorlton, and Porto

    A terrace in Chorlton with an old housemate again, nearly four years on. The first night was the fifteenth of May, arriving late.

    And Porto, repeatedly and for a reason.

    The move is planned for the sixteenth of October. The record ends at now; the plan carries on past it.
